headline: Recommended City Council approval of Hope House funding from Jill C. Duson Housing Trust Fund, with 30-year affordability covenant.
summary: Councilors heard a rent control report and discussed changes to the rent control ordinance. They asked staff for a red-lined version to review in September. The committee also discussed tax increment financing changes for affordable housing and ways to support the arts, and went into executive session on city property at Portland Technology Park.
decisions: Amended the Hope House funding request to set the affordability covenant at 30 years, unanimously.
Recommended City Council approval of the Hope House funding request from the Jill C. Duson Housing Trust Fund, with a 30-year covenant, 4-0.
Requested a red-lined version of the rent control ordinance amendments, with review targeted for September.

plain_text:
1 
MINUTES 
HOUSING AND ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT COMMITTEE 
Date: July 21, 2026 at 5:30 pm  
NOTE: This meeting was held via Zoom and can be viewed at this link: 
https://portlandme.portal.civicclerk.com/event/8215/media 
These minutes provide a record of those in attendance, general discussions that took 
place and motions made. 
Attendance: 
Council and Committee Members: Councilor Pious Ali, Chair, and members Councilors 
Regina Phillips, Sarah Michniewicz, Kate Sykes, and Councilor Wes Pelletier. 
Staff: Dena Libner, Assistant City Manager, Amy McNally, Associate Corporation 
Counsel, Jessica Quattropani, Permitting and Inspections Director, Mary Davis, Housing 
and Community Development Division Director, Heidi McCarthy, Housing Program 
Manager, Lori Paulette, Principal Administrative Officer, Nancy Martin, Business 
Programs Manager 
A G E N D A 
1. Review and vote to approve meeting Minutes from the June 30, 2026,
meeting.
Motion to approve: Councilor Sykes 
Second: Councilor Michniewicz 
Passed 4-0 
2. Communication: Quarter 2 (4/1/2026 - 6/30/2026) Rent Control Report -
Jessica Quattropani, Permitting and Inspections Department Director
Director Quattropani presented a summary of the Rent Control Report for
Quarter 2 and answered questions from councilors.
Are we auditing newer buildings? Random audits are given for new and old
properties which haven't been audited within the past year.
What is a partially registered unit and how long does it take to resolve, and
are those units occupied? Partially registered means that they have either
paid or turned in registration documents, but not both. They may have 30
days to pay, the units are likely occupied.
Clarification on unfounded complaints: Not a violation of ordinance, but
may be violation of state law. All get referred to Pine Tree Legal. A request
was made to change the name.
FINAL July 21, 2026 HEDC Meeting Minutes
Approved September 15, 2026
2 
 
 
 
3. Discussion: Amendments to Rent Control Ordinance to Strengthen 
Enforcement - Councilor Pious Ali, Chair 
 
Councilor Ali provided background on the purpose of this item. Corporation 
Counsel’s memo has highlighted some legal challenges and stated that it 
would be helpful to clarify portions of the ordinance to mitigate legal 
challenges in the future.  
 
Committee members discussed the changes and expressed support for 
clarifying the definitions and timeline for paying back residents.   
 
A Councilor expressed concern about creating loopholes with the changes. 
The Committee discussed next steps which could include passing 
straightforward changes and allowing for more substantial changes as well. 
In addition to those presented tonight, there may be other changes the 
Committee wishes to make, including strengthening eviction prevention, 
increasing record keeping, and providing complete information to the Rent 
Board. The Committee requested a red-lined version of the ordinance to 
include previous suggestions by staff, and the process should be done 
through the Committee process of reviewing a red-lined version, targeting  
September, then potentially inviting stakeholders to comment.  
 
4. Discussion: Consider policy to enhance public support for the arts - 
Councilor Pious Ali, Chair 
 
Ms. Libner noted there was no memo or backup for this item as staff is 
seeking Committee guidance about policy action and what public support 
looks like.  After that guidance is given, Corporation Counsel and staff can 
flesh this out, including what other municipalities the size of Portland might 
offer. 
 
Councilor Sykes noted that perhaps a new Cultural Plan is overdue.  This 
should occur but not sure if HEDC is the appropriate venue for that project.  
Past cultural plans may help provide a framework for discussion purposes, 
including arts that are new and their needs today. 
Chair Councilor Ali noted the Federal Government is cutting back on art-
related funding, and the Committee could discuss potential new resources 
for the arts outside of the box or improve known resources.   
Councilor Michniewicz noted the entertainment fund with the new 
ordinance would tie into support for the arts.  She also noted that it would be 
helpful if staff could draft a memo that highlights how we currently support 
the arts and where the gaps may be – this would be helpful to start the
3 
 
discussion.  She would like to be able to support galleries, music venues, and 
the like. 
Ms. Libner said that staff could start to flesh out past plans, what is currently 
being done, what could be done – i.e., entertainment fund, and provide that 
for further discussion for policy action ideas from the Committee. 
5. Public Comment: Review and possible recommendation to the City Council 
amendments to the City’s Tax Increment Financing Policy - Mary Davis, 
Housing and Community Development Director, Heidi McCarthy, Housing 
Program Manager 
 
Ms. McCarthy provided an overview of suggested amendments, including 
changes to the underwriting process for Affordable Housing (AH) TIF 
projects, and clarifying definitions.  She noted that as part of Qualified 
Allocation Plan (QAP) process by the Maine State Housing Authority (MSHA) 
for distribution of Low-Incomedistribution Low-Income Housing Tax 
Credits (LIHTC), the proposed amendments would help to streamline 
Portland’s process.  She then described the rationale for the amendments, 
which could save both time and money for the developers by using inhouse 
underwriting for those projects going through the QAP process. 
 
There was clarification about whether taking a vote at this meeting was 
needed, and staff noted that it would not hold up projects if there was no 
vote today. 
 
The Committee discussed the proposed amendments with thoughts that 
taking away the third-party underwriter may not be good for the City, but 
that if there are routine applications that could be underwritten in house 
versus complex, higher risk applications could go to a third-party 
underwriter. 
 
Ms. Davis noted that most AHTIF applications use the TIF revenue for 
operating costs after the development is built, while there are very few who 
use TIF revenues for the construction phase.  This proposed amendment is 
targeted to developers who will use TIF revenue for operating costs, and, 
therefore, inhouse underwriting would save time and funds.  Operating costs 
cover such things as maintenance, utilities, property management, debt 
service, trash removal and the like.  For AHTIF applications where TIF 
revenue would be used for construction costs, those would go to a third-
party underwriter.  Perhaps this could be better articulated in the TIF policy. 
 
There followed discussion about processes with LIHTC and QAP, as well use 
of TIF funds for operating costs versus construction costs.  In either case, if 
the development does not happen, there is no TIF revenue to use.  The 
Committee would like the City to have in the policy the ability to separate
4 
 
out complex projects for a third-party underwriter to undertake and also to 
allow the City flexibility to determine when a third-party underwriter 
should be utilized for a project, particularly should this Committee or the 
Council raiseraises a concern with a particular project. 
 
Ms. Davis noted the direction and staff would come back with a proposal to 
reflect the discussion today.  
 
6. Public Comment: Review and recommendation to the City Council of a 
request for funding from the Jill C. Duson Housing Trust Fund re: Hope 
Acts, Hope House - Mary Davis, Housing and Community Development 
Director, Heidi McCarthy, Housing Program Manager 
 
Ms. McCarthy highlighted the item noting that this funding request would 
support the ongoing rehabilitation of the Hope House, serving asylum 
seekers.  They had a successful capital fundraising campaign and began the 
renovation process.  Demolition uncovered issues with the building’s 
foundation and framing which is what the bulk of the funds they are 
requesting would be used for, as well as $78K to support solar installation.  
She noted that if solar is installed by the end of this year, a tax credit would 
pay for 30% of the system, which would provide 63% of the building’s 
electricity needs.  
 
There were clarifying questions such as if this was too much for a CDBG 
grant and it was, as well as the timing for the next round of CDBG 
applications starting in October with the renovations currently ongoing.  In 
addition, there was discussion of the City funds perhaps not being used for 
housing purposes - with further discussion noting that the services in the 
basement are a part of the overall operating facet of the Hope House, 
including a community space and programmatic support for the residents to 
deliver services and stay housed. 
 
Chair Ali then opened the meeting for public comment.   
 
Dan Black, Portland resident and development consultant on this project, 
noted that this funding is very necessary and required to make the building 
habitable in the future to provide housing and services. 
 
Martha Stein, Executive Director of Hope House, thanked the Committee for 
their time in responding to this request.  The Hope House would have never 
opened in the first place without the support of its Founders and the City of 
Portland.  She noted that residents have access to the staff in the lower level, 
including the use of computers, office equipment, activities, workshops, 
classes and space for services for asylum seekers, work permit preparation
5 
 
that staff assists with, and open office hours.  She thanked the Committee 
for their time. 
 
Seeing no further public comment, Chair Councilor Ali closed the public 
comment session. 
 
The Committee expressed their support for the Hope House with consensus 
to recommend approval, but with affordability covenants at 30 years. 
 
Councilor Sykes made a motion to amend the affordabilityamend 
affordability covenant from 15 years to 30 years.  Councilor Phillips seconded 
the motion and it passed unanimously. 
 
Councilor Sykes then made a motion to recommend to the City Council 
approval of this request, including increasing the affordability covenant 
from 15 years to 30 years.  Councilor Michniewicz seconded the motion and 
it passed 4-0. 
 
7. Executive Session: Pursuant to M.R.S.A. 405(6)(C) and 5 M.R.S.A. 13119-A, 
the Committee will go into executive session to provide staff direction 
regarding possible negotiation for sale of City-owned property at Portland 
Technology Park - Dena Libner, Assistant City Manager, Nancy Martin, 
Business Programs Manager 
 
On motion made by Councilor Pelletier, seconded by Councilor Sykes, the 
Committee voted 4-0 at 7:53 p.m. to go into executive session as noted 
above.   
 
At approximately 8:15 p.m. the Committee came out of executive session. 
 
On motion then made by Councilor Sykes, seconded by Councilor Phillips, 
the Committee voted 4-0 to adjourn the meeting. 
 
 
Next meeting date: September 15, 2026
